newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Airlines to ease compensation limit for crashes.
newsitem.headline: Airlines to ease compensation limit for crashes.

text.p: The International Air Transport Association (IATA) said Tuesday it expects many world carriers to begin removing limits on compensation for victims of air disasters and their dependents beginning in January.

An industry accord, which has been stalled by a dispute over its terms between IATA and the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), means airlines will move quickly after a crash to negotiate "reasonable and just" payments, a spokesman said.

He was speaking after five major European airlines and four small regional carriers announced they would accept unlimited liability, abandoning ceilings for accident compensation set after World War II and widely seen as too low and outdated.
"We expect other major airlines to follow suit in the coming weeks, and that many of the big companies will be on board by the New Year," IATA spokesman Tim Goodyear said.
IATA, which has 253 members and is based in Geneva and Montreal, has set Jan. 1, 1997, as the target for the accord to come into force.
It has been signed by 77 airlines, representing more than 80 percent of scheduled international air traffic and including nearly all major global carriers.

The airline body initially aimed for implementation as of Nov. 1, but terms at first imposed by the U.S. transportation agent, which supervises the world's biggest single civil aviation market, led to a postponement.

The five European carriers -- Austrian Airlines, Finnair, Dutch KLM, Scandivania's SAS and Swissair -- as well as Switzerland's Crossair, Dutch KLM Cityhopper, Martinair and Transavia, indicated they would apply the pact immediately.

"Governments have spent 30 years trying to achieve sensible modifications to the Warsaw system. The airlines are now doing it voluntarily," IATA Director-General Pierre Jeanniot said, welcoming the decision by the five.

At present, under the industry's 1929 Warsaw Convention, airlines are restricted to compensation payments -- varying from country to country -- which specialist lawyers say are "grossly inadequate and unsustainable."
The limits range from $75,000 in the United States to $150,000 in Europe and $350,000 in Australia.

To obtain more, injured crash victims or the families of the dead have had to engage in costly court proceedings, often stretching out over months and even years, to prove negligence on the part of the company involved.
Under the accord, the Inter-Carrier Agreement on Passenger Liability, airlines will negotiate promptly with victims' relatives or their lawyers to agree on a sum to be paid.
"It means that instead of having to go through the extra trauma of a court case to get fair compensation, people affected will have the prospect of a quick settlement," Goodyear said.

Airlines themselves have long chafed at the inter-governmental Warsaw Convention limits as legal costs for judicial hearings have soared, especially in the United States. They have been usually capped by large out-of-court settlements.
